prize_parts.citation: For elucidating the structure and mechanism of nitrogenase, the enzyme that reduces dinitrogen to ammonia.

statement.case_for: Nitrogenase is a first-rank problem in fundamental chemical mechanism: how a metalloenzyme couples ATP-driven electron delivery to the six-electron reduction of N2 under ambient conditions. The field has delivered a defined cofactor architecture (FeMo-cofactor with its interstitial carbide), a kinetic framework for the electron-transfer and ATP-hydrolysis cycle, and more recently structures of turnover states. This is the kind of physically stated mechanism, built from kinetics, spectroscopy and structure together, that I think the prize should reward. It also bears on a long-standing question for agriculture and for energy chemistry, and it has not been recognised before. Structures have been confirmed by several independent groups, so the structural half of the achievement is mature even if the catalytic half is still open.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the catalytic mechanism at the cofactor is not closed: the E4 hydride state, the N2 binding site and the role of sulfur displacement are still debated, and a prize could be called premature for the mechanism part. Credit is also spread over at least five people (Dean, Rees, Seefeldt, Einsle, Ribbe), and a three-person limit forces an unsatisfying cut that leaves out the genetics and cofactor-biosynthesis line. B012 also drew first place from only one member, so I cannot claim broad support.

responses.point: Johan ranks base editing first and would give the prize to David Liu alone, calling it a chemist's invention that is already clinical and that avoids a split with CRISPR-Cas9.
responses.response: I agree that base editing is a real conceptual advance and that Liu is the intellectual driver. But a Liu-alone citation sits uneasily with the credited names on the ballot: Komor and Gaudelli are the first authors of the two editor classes, and Kondo and Nishida published an independent deaminase fusion. The committee will have to explain why those claims fall away. I also share Johan's own caveat that clinical durability and safety data are still accumulating. I keep B062 as my first alternative, but I want the expert report on attribution before I rank it above a mechanistic problem that has been studied for decades.

responses.point: Heiner ranks Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first. He sees a clear, general principle with enormous industrial use, easy to explain, and a clean two-person prize for Buchwald and Hartwig.
responses.response: I accept that the attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist and that the maturity is not in question. My reservation is the one Heiner names himself: the 2010 cross-coupling prize already recognised the general logic of Pd-catalysed coupling, and a C-N citation risks reading as an extension of that rather than a new principle. I would ask the expert reports whether the ligand-design contribution is distinct enough from 2010 to stand on its own. I do not put B039 in my configuration, but if that question is answered convincingly I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Emma ranks biomolecular condensates first, as a physically grounded concept of membraneless organisation, with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as the natural trio.
responses.response: The physical-chemical framing is attractive, and I take seriously her point that this reorganised how cell biochemistry is thought about. I qualify it in two ways. First, her own uncertainty list notes that the physiological relevance and the liquid-versus-gel character of many condensates are still contested. That is a closer analogue to my maturity worry on nitrogenase than I would like to admit, but here the debate concerns whether the phenomenon is functionally what is claimed, not just its detailed mechanism. Second, Pappu and Mittag supplied much of the sequence-grammar and quantitative framework, and leaving them out is a real attribution cost. I am not convinced B036 is a chemistry achievement as opposed to cell biology.

responses.point: Daniel ranks targeted protein degradation first, as a new drug modality with Crews, Deshaies and Handa as the core, and he concedes that the three-person cut is contestable.
responses.response: I agree with the concession. PROTACs and molecular glues rest on different discoveries, and Aqvist, Aili and Chabes each name a different trio, which shows how unsettled the attribution is. Handa's identification of cereblon is the easiest part to defend mechanistically. The remaining question is whether Crews and Deshaies, or Ciulli and Gray, carry the PROTAC half, and whether a bifunctional degrader without regulatory approval is mature enough. I see B066 as the strongest candidate that is not mine, and it is my second alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the E4 hydride and N2-binding mechanism is settled enough to be described as understood, or whether the citation should be limited to structure and the electron-transfer framework.
Whether three of Dean, Rees, Seefeldt, Einsle and Ribbe can be chosen without leaving out an equally decisive contribution.
Whether the expert reports separate the base-editing credit of Liu, Komor, Gaudelli, Kondo and Nishida clearly enough to support a three-person prize.
I have not verified the details of the most recent cryo-EM turnover structures and am relying on memory.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the nitrogenase candidates. My own field (respiratory enzymes, proton and electron transfer) is adjacent to metalloenzyme mechanism, which is an interest rather than a personal connection, and I will keep it in mind so as not to overweight bioenergetics. I am a Stockholm University colleague of Xiaodong Zou; none of the shortlisted candidates in my configuration is linked to that.
